questions.prompt: What's the difference between a slash command and a regular prompt?

options.text: Slash commands are prompts written more politely
A prompt goes into the conversation for Claude to act on; a slash command steers the session itself — clearing it, resuming one, changing settings
Slash commands are only for programmers

questions.explanation: The conversation is the cargo; slash commands drive the truck. /clear, /resume, and /config manage the session around Claude rather than asking Claude to do something — the leading / is how the app tells the two apart.

questions.prompt: You spent an hour fixing a bug, and now you're starting a completely unrelated task in the same project. What's the best first move?

options.text: /clear — start fresh so the old task's context doesn't drag into the new one
Keep going in the same conversation — more context is always better

questions.explanation: An unrelated task deserves a clean slate: the bug hunt's long history is now noise that steers responses off course. 'More context is always better' (c) is the classic trap — RELEVANT context helps; leftover context pollutes. This is module 02's 'restart beats a fifth correction' with a button on it.

questions.prompt: Yesterday you and Claude got halfway through reorganizing a project. Today you want to continue exactly where you left off. Which command?

options.text: /resume — pick yesterday's session and continue with its full memory intact
No command needed — Claude automatically remembers all past conversations

questions.explanation: /resume lists past sessions and reopens the one you pick, history and all — 'the second file, like we discussed' works again. Memory across sessions is opt-in, not automatic (d): a fresh session starts blank except for CLAUDE.md, which is exactly why /resume exists.

questions.prompt: You can't remember what commands exist or what one of them does. What do you type?
questions.explanation: /help lists every available command with what it does — it's the one command worth memorizing precisely because it makes memorizing the rest optional. /clear (b) would wipe your session, which is a rough way to look something up.
